points.t: High fever, headache behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and a flushing or ‘white islands’ rash, within 2 weeks of tropical travel.
Dengue virus spread by *Aedes* mosquitoes; capillary leak and low platelets drive severe disease, often as the fever falls.
Same-day assessment: malaria test, FBC (platelets, haematocrit), dengue NS1/serology; paracetamol and fluids only; notifiable.
Severe dengue (plasma leakage, bleeding, organ impairment), and NSAIDs or aspirin increasing bleeding risk.

points: **Aetiology:** dengue virus is a **flavivirus** (same family as yellow fever and Zika). It is a single-stranded RNA virus with **four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4)**.
Incubation is **4–10 days** (range about 3–14). A patient can infect feeding mosquitoes during the viraemic phase.

**Immunity:** infection gives lifelong immunity to that serotype and only brief cross-protection to the others. **Antibody-dependent enhancement** at a later infection with a different serotype is thought to drive more severe disease.

**Skin mechanisms:** capillary dilatation causes the early flush. An immune-mediated viral exanthem causes the morbilliform rash. **Thrombocytopenia, capillary fragility and endothelial leak** cause petechiae and purpura.

**Febrile phase (days 1–3/7):** abrupt high fever, severe **frontal/retro-orbital headache**, **myalgia, arthralgia and back pain ("break-bone fever")**, nausea and vomiting, and a positive tourniquet test.
**Critical phase (around defervescence, days 3–7):** plasma leakage can develop **as the fever settles**. This is the danger window.
**Recovery phase:** fluid reabsorbs, and there may be bradycardia and the convalescent rash.
**Early (first 24–48 h):** transient **flushing/blanching erythema** of the face, neck and chest.
**Days 3–6:** a **maculopapular or morbilliform exanthem**. It often starts on the dorsum of the hands and feet, spreads to the limbs and trunk, and may be itchy.

**Haemorrhagic signs:** **petechiae** (especially on the **lower legs**, feet and at pressure sites), purpura/ecchymoses, conjunctival injection or bleeding, gum bleeding and nosebleeds. A **positive tourniquet test** shows capillary fragility.
fever plus travel to an endemic area within the past 2 weeks (dengue's incubation fits returns within about 14 days). **Always exclude malaria first** if the patient travelled to a malarious area.
FBC: **leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, rising haematocrit**; LFTs: raised transaminases; U&E, CRP (usually low or modest)
dengue virus is a laboratory-notifiable organism in England. Clinicians do not need to notify suspected cases.
Serology **cross-reacts** with other flaviviruses (Zika, yellow fever/Japanese encephalitis vaccines), so give the full travel and vaccine history.

cards.name: Malaria
cards.clue: **Exclude urgently** in any febrile returnee from a malarious area (same-day thick/thin films or RDT). Usually no rash

cards.name: Chikungunya
cards.clue: Same *Aedes* vector. **Severe, persistent polyarthralgia/arthritis** dominates; haemorrhage and shock are rare

cards.name: Zika
cards.clue: Milder fever, **itchy rash, conjunctivitis**; pregnancy implications

cards.name: Rickettsial infection (African tick-bite fever, scrub/murine typhus, RMSF)
cards.clue: **Eschar**, regional lymphadenopathy; vesicular/petechial rash on palms/soles (RMSF). Responds to doxycycline

cards.name: Meningococcal septicaemia
cards.clue: **Non-blanching purpuric rash + unwell** = emergency, treat immediately

cards.name: Measles / rubella
cards.clue: Coryza, cough, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots; cephalocaudal spread; check vaccination status

cards.name: Acute HIV seroconversion
cards.clue: Morbilliform rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, oral ulcers; sexual history

cards.name: Typhoid / leptospirosis
cards.clue: Rose spots (typhoid); freshwater exposure, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice/renal failure (leptospirosis)

cards.name: COVID-19
cards.clue: Can also cause **purpuric/petechial** and morbilliform eruptions

cards.name: Drug eruption (incl. DRESS)
cards.clue: New drug 1–8 weeks before; eosinophilia, facial oedema

items.t: **Warning signs**: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, fluid accumulation, rising haematocrit with falling platelets: emergency admission.
Never give **NSAIDs or aspirin** in suspected dengue.
Fever after the tropics: exclude **malaria** the same day.

pearls.t: **A second dengue infection carries a higher risk of severe disease.** Previously infected travellers deserve a careful pre-travel consultation.
Dengue cannot be caught person to person in the UK (no established vector), apart from rare blood/organ/vertical transmission.
